title: One yoke lightens others (Avot 3:5)
hookLine: Nechunia: take on the yoke of Torah, and other burdens are lifted
tomorrow: what if there's no one to study with?

lines: TAKE ON A YOKE, LOSE TWO.
cards: Calendar like a game of Tetris. Rehearsal, a paper, a shift, a birthday, three group chats all waiting on an answer. The advice is always the same: drop something.
So can taking on more ever make life feel lighter? Rabbi Nechunia ben HaKanah says yes, if it's the right thing.
Whoever takes on the yoke of Torah, he says in Avot, has the yoke of the government and the yoke of worldly cares taken off him. Whoever throws it off has them laid on.

teach.b: Today's question: how can one more thing make the load lighter? Start with the picture. A yoke is a wooden beam across an animal's shoulders.
It doesn't add weight so much as gather it, so the pull goes through one place instead of everywhere at once. Nechunia's answer is that a person carries something either way.
Take on Torah, its study and its commandments, and the other loads find their place under it.

teach.h: TORAH, OR THE LOADS COME BACK.
teach.b: Throw it off, and the same loads come back unorganized, and heavier. The same picture appears in Jewish prayer.

teach.h: THE SHEMA: A YOKE CHOSEN DAILY.
teach.b: The Mishnah says that saying the Shema is accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven, and only then the yoke of the commandments. A yoke chosen every morning. Now a neighbor.
In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says, "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light."
Shared ground: a chosen yoke that makes the rest lighter, rest found by taking something on.
An honest difference: for Nechunia, the yoke is Torah, the teaching and its commandments; in Matthew, Jesus invites people to take on his own yoke and learn from him.
Neighbors using the same farm tool, each in their own words.

how: Jews traditionally say the Shema morning and evening, described in the Mishnah as accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven, and take on regular study, such as a daily page or a weekly class.

games.q: what does “one yoke lightens others” mean?
o: a chosen commitment that lifts other burdens
a heavy rule that adds to everything you carry
a promise to give up all worldly work

p: take on Torah, lose the other yokes

taking it on removes other yokes, Nechunia says; throwing it off brings them back.

games.q: your cousin is drowning in deadlines and says adding a weekly study hour is the last thing he needs. what does Nechunia's saying suggest?
o: one chosen commitment can put the other loads in order.
drop every commitment so nothing sits on your shoulders.
say yes to everything asked of you, to prove you can.
games.why: Nechunia says the yoke of Torah lifts other yokes. the point isn't more weight; it's one chosen beam that gathers the rest.

practice: Name one small commitment that could steady the rest: ten minutes of reading at the same hour, a weekly call to someone older, a meal with no phones.
Say the wish to yourself, then the thing most likely to get in its way, then the plan: when that happens, I will… Hold the plan quietly until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: One yoke lightens others: Nechunia's saying that the yoke of Torah, taken on freely, lifts the yokes of the world.

orig.note: Hebrew: the yoke of Torah, Avot 3:5.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: one yoke lightens others, when it's the one you chose. Until tomorrow, then.
